channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] The water campaign, one month on: 100+ exposed systems, and an attack surface no asset register had recorded
item.description: A month on, July’s wave against US water utilities is the best-documented OT campaign of the year, and CISA has put a figure on it: malicious activity against more than 100 internet-exposed systems in the Water and Wastewater Systems sector, commonly programmable logic controllers wired straight into a cellular modem, across at least a dozen states. The FBI records incidents at utilities in at least seven states since 27 July, some degrading operations — lost pressure, flooding, forced manual running — though service was not widely interrupted. The government links the activity to Iranian actors and says it targeted operational technology rather than data. What makes this the board’s most useful item is the admission behind the number: the exposure that enabled it was never in anybody’s asset register. CISA’s guidance applies to every sector — scan yourself from the outside, then remove what operations do not require. - CISA Exposure Reduction guidance — corroborated by SecurityWeek, TechCrunch and The Register - Guidance published and reported 26 Aug 2026; observed activity July 2026; FBI PSA 30 Jul 2026; re-verified 28 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Boston Scientific, day four: shifts cancelled at three Irish plants, and a hacktivist crew has now claimed it
item.description: Updated 28 August: on day four the picture has hardened in two ways. Production is now visibly affected — day-shift workers at the Model Farm Road plant in Cork, roughly 1,200 people, were sent home on full pay, with staff at Clonmel and Galway offered leave, from a workforce of more than 7,000 across the three Irish sites. And a pro-Russian hacktivist crew calling itself Server Killers has claimed the attack; Boston Scientific has not confirmed that claim, named an entry route, or said whether ransomware or data theft is involved, and hacktivist claims of this kind frequently do not survive scrutiny. The company confirmed on 26 August, in a statement and an SEC filing, that an intrusion identified on 25 August is disrupting operations worldwide, including its ability to process and ship customer orders; analysts at Piper Sandler put full restoration at up to three weeks. Nothing has been confirmed about plant-floor control systems. That distinction is the lesson rather than the reassurance it looks like: order management, warehouse and shipping systems sit outside most OT programmes, yet losing them stops product moving just as effectively as stopping a line. - Boston Scientific statement and SEC filing — reported by BleepingComputer, Cybersecurity Dive, TechCrunch, The Register and CBS News; Cork, Clonmel and Galway shift detail via the Irish Examiner and Silicon Republic; actor claim reported by SecurityWeek; restoration estimate via a Piper Sandler analyst note - Detected 25 Aug 2026; disclosed 26 Aug 2026; still disrupted — updated 28 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] The S7 advisory’s real finding: attackers are running AI-written exploitation scripts dressed up as OT monitoring tools
item.description: Joint advisory AA26-231A, published 19 August by NSA, CISA, the FBI, DOE and EPA, says threat actors are running AI-generated Python scripts — packaged to look like ordinary OT monitoring software — to find and reach Siemens S7 controllers across US critical infrastructure. The tooling is built on the snap7.dll and python-snap7 libraries and speaks S7comm, giving read and write access to PLC memory, configuration data and ladder logic. Targets are located through internet-wide scanning services such as Censys and ZoomEye, then reached through exposed interfaces, outdated firmware or weak authentication. S7-200, S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200 and S7-1500 are all named — including F-series safety controllers — across critical manufacturing, energy, water and wastewater, chemical, food and agriculture, and commercial facilities. The agencies assess the activity as persistent reconnaissance and capability development positioning actors for later disruption, say the targeting is broader than Siemens, and state plainly that this is not a theoretical risk. They also flag a blind spot worth acting on: where a system integrator or MSP holds remote access, the asset owner frequently does not know the controller is internet-reachable at all. The related campaign against water-sector controllers is where the confirmed damage sits — attackers modified or deleted project-file logic, manipulated HMI and SCADA display data, and disabled shutdown and alarm functions, creating unsafe conditions with no operator notification. - NSA / CISA / FBI / DOE / EPA joint advisory AA26-231A, building on AA26-097A and the FBI water-sector alert — via CISA, BleepingComputer, The Hacker News and Industrial Cyber - AA26-231A published 19 Aug 2026 (advisory PDF posted 18 Aug), re-verified 26 Aug 2026 12:35 PM ET; FBI water-sector alert 4 Aug 2026; campaign ongoing since 27 Jul 2026

item.title: [Critical] UK government confirms a cyberattack took a generator offline — and is rewriting the sector’s cyber rules
item.description: A small UK gas-fired generating site was taken offline for four days, in what officials describe as the first successful cyberattack of its kind on British energy infrastructure. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero confirms a cyberattack impacted a small-scale energy generator, stresses the national grid and customer supply were never at risk, and — the part defenders should note — says sector cybersecurity regulations are now being updated. The four-day duration and the Iran attribution remain press-sourced, carried by the Telegraph and picked up widely; the NCSC has not commented and the facility has not been named. The affected site sat below the threshold at which generators must report cyber incidents. That exposed population is embedded generation, CHP and district energy, standby and peaking plant, battery storage and small renewables — unmanned assets reached through vendor remote access or a cellular router, sitting under the regulatory floor. The disclosure landed the same week the US Treasury sanctioned Iranian nationals over intrusions at energy companies, which is why the two stories are being read together even though neither government has joined them. - On-record statement from the UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, reported via SecurityWeek, The Record and Help Net Security; duration and attribution from the Sunday Telegraph - Telegraph report published 22 Aug 2026; DESNZ statement 23 Aug 2026; trade-press pickup 24 Aug 2026; re-verified 26 Aug 2026 with no new technical detail released; attack occurred July 2026, exact date not published

item.title: [Critical] US seizes the Chinese state-sponsored scanning and relay network built out of other people’s IoT devices
item.description: The Justice Department and FBI announced on 26 August that they had seized the domains behind QScan and QTRouter, two linked platforms operated by a PRC state-sponsored group DOJ tracks as QTFY and ties to a Nanjing technology company. QScan automatically scans for and infects internet-facing IoT devices worldwide; QTRouter then enrols those devices, alongside commercial proxy services and leased virtual private servers, into a network that hides the Chinese origin of intrusions. DOJ says the service was sold on to customers including China’s Ministry of State Security and the People’s Liberation Army. Named victims include NASA, the Federal Reserve, the Department of Energy, HHS and the US Senate, with power companies, hospitals, telecoms and defence contractors among private targets. Because the seized domains were hard-coded into both malware families, the takedown rendered them inoperable. For OT operators the uncomfortable part is the raw material rather than the target list: the cameras, cellular gateways and routers sitting unmanaged at remote sites are exactly what this infrastructure is built from. - US Department of Justice press release and court documents — corroborated by CNBC and ITPro - Announced 26 Aug 2026; verified against the DOJ release the same day

item.title: [Critical] Washington sanctions an Iranian cyber network inside US critical infrastructure — but not the crew touching the controllers
item.description: Treasury designated a Ministry of Intelligence and Security–directed hacking group on 24 August, and the detail matters more than the headline: the network named is an espionage and theft cluster, not the one manipulating process equipment. Treasury says its members — five of them indicted by the Justice Department the week before — have been breaching and exfiltrating data from US energy companies, defence contractors, healthcare providers, IT firms and banks since at least late 2023. That is access collection, and the same footholds convert to disruption when tasking changes. Running alongside it, still formally unattributed by CISA, is the campaign that has degraded water operations across at least a dozen states through internet-facing controllers. The State Department has posted a reward notice on the wider problem. Two clusters, one adversary, one of them named — and the naming changes your legal position long before it changes your exposure. - US Treasury press release and OFAC designations; State Department Rewards for Justice notice; reported via The Record, Nextgov/FCW and The Hacker News - Designations announced 24 Aug 2026; DOJ indictments the preceding week; trade-press analysis 25 Aug 2026; re-verified 26 Aug 2026 — no further designations or CISA attribution issued

item.title: [High] CERT Polska’s post-mortem names the entry point nobody was watching: the utility’s own private cellular APN
item.description: CERT Polska published its follow-up report on 8 August, closing a three-month investigation into the 29 December 2025 attacks on Polish energy assets, and the finding is the reason this belongs on a 2026 dashboard rather than a 2025 one. The attackers reached the OT network of a combined heat and power plant through a private APN — the dedicated mobile network a distribution system operator provisions with a carrier to reach its own field equipment. CERT Polska describes this as the first case it has observed of that route being used to get into an OT network. Inside, the intruders shut down a steam turbine and the water treatment system producing process water, interrupting cogeneration at a plant serving roughly 50,000 residents; heat and power supply to customers was not lost. The same 29 December wave hit more than 30 wind and photovoltaic sites and a manufacturer. CERT Polska characterises the objective as destructive rather than financial. Read alongside the US water campaign — PLCs sitting on cellular modems — the pattern is the same one: carrier-provided connectivity that the operator treats as private, and therefore never firewalls, monitors or inventories. - CERT Polska follow-up incident report — corroborated by Help Net Security and The Hacker News - Incident 29 Dec 2025; CERT Polska follow-up report published 8 Aug 2026; coverage 11 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] CISA ran the same attack against a water utility and a government body — one caught it, the other never noticed
item.description: Advisory AA26-237A, published on 25 August, reports two simultaneous CISA red-team assessments run with comparable tradecraft against two critical-infrastructure organisations. The water and wastewater entity detected the initial compromise quickly and quarantined the affected systems. The government services organisation did not: the team landed on four workstations after finding a web application still using default credentials for built-in accounts, phished from an internal address, took domain privileges, and moved into sensitive business systems and cloud resources without triggering a response — eventually reading the security team’s own email and putting keyloggers on defenders’ machines. CISA’s explanation is the part worth circulating internally. Thousands of false positives from routine business activity, many rated high, buried the real alerts. Multiple SOCs and endpoint tools ran with no shared visibility. Analysts had neither escalation procedures nor authority to act. A genuine alert on a configuration-management server was closed as a false positive because nobody could work out who owned the box. - CISA advisory AA26-237A — corroborated by CyberScoop and The Hacker News - Published 25 Aug 2026; verified against the CISA advisory 26 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] 4,407 controllers are answering from the public internet — and 22 of them sit in the towns being attacked
item.description: Forescout’s Vedere Labs scanned for controllers responding on EtherNet/IP port 44818 and found 4,407 exposed worldwide on 3 August, 2,844 of them in the United States, with Canada and Spain next. Twenty-two of those hosts were in cities named in the ongoing water-utility campaign, and 19 of the 22 ran firmware susceptible to a Modbus TCP buffer overflow in MicroLogix 1400 Series B/C that Rockwell patched in 2017. The exposed population is dominated by MicroLogix 1400 — about half the total — followed by CompactLogix 1769, MicroLogix 1100 and ControlLogix 5590. The finding that should change procurement conversations: roughly 70% of the US devices reach the internet through large mobile-carrier networks, meaning cellular routers at pump stations, lift stations and unstaffed field sites. Total exposure is down 47% from a 2020 peak, and Forescout characterises the observed attacks as opportunistic exploitation at scale rather than a sophisticated targeted operation — which is the uncomfortable part, because it means the barrier to disrupting a US water utility is currently very low. - Forescout Research — Vedere Labs analysis — via Forescout, The Hacker News and CyberScoop - Scan performed 3 Aug 2026; research published 6 Aug 2026; re-verified 26 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] 1,140 industrial ransomware victims in a quarter — and not one attacker needed to touch a control system
item.description: Dragos recorded 1,140 ransomware incidents against industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up 12% on the first quarter, with manufacturing absorbing 747 of them, construction 176, equipment manufacturing 114 and food and beverage 70. The headline finding for OT teams is what did not happen: Dragos observed no case in the quarter where a ransomware operator reached Stage 2 of the ICS Cyber Kill Chain or directly manipulated a control system. Where operations stopped, it followed encryption of — or precautionary shutdown because of — the enterprise IT, ERP and virtualisation layers that production depends on. Tradecraft stayed consistent: exploitation of internet-facing edge devices and remote-management tooling, abuse of valid accounts, credential theft, and EDR-killer plus bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver techniques ahead of impact. Extortion continues drifting from encryption toward data theft, so exposure persists after restoration. Dragos now tracks 119 ransomware groups touching industrial targets, up from 80 in 2024. - Dragos Industrial Ransomware Analysis, Q2 2026 — via Dragos and Help Net Security - Report covers Q2 2026; published and reported 11 Aug 2026; re-verified 26 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] CVSS 10.0 on a Siemens edge gateway — the Node-RED interface takes commands from anyone who can reach it
item.description: Siemens’ August Patch Tuesday set, published 12 August and picked up in the CISA batch the following day, carries a maximum-severity entry: CVE-2026-58115, CVSS 10.0, in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced. The device ships a Node-RED HTTP interface that does not enforce authentication, and Node-RED’s programming nodes can run system commands. So an unauthenticated attacker who can reach the interface can author a flow and execute code on the device with maximum privileges — no credential, no exploit chain, just the product working as configured. Siemens has published fixed firmware and points operators to the Node-RED hardening guidance. The IoT2050 is used across chemical, critical manufacturing, energy and transportation, and it earns its place on this list because of where it sits: these gateways are deployed precisely to bridge process data out of the plant, which means one of their interfaces usually faces the business network. The same Siemens set also fixed a critical code-execution flaw in Siveillance Video Management Servers; Schneider Electric issued advisories for NetBotz 5 and PowerChute Serial Shutdown. No public exploitation of CVE-2026-58115 has been reported. - Siemens ProductCERT August 2026 advisories and CISA ICS advisory batch — reported by SecurityWeek - Published 12 Aug 2026; re-verified 26 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Ten flaws, CVSS 9.8, no login required and no patch coming — and CISA has now flagged a second Ebyte gateway
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-237-06 on 25 August covering ten vulnerabilities in the Ebyte NE2-D11 serial-to-Ethernet gateway, firmware FW-9167-0-11. The web management interface does not enforce authentication on administrative functions (CVE-2026-73125, CVSS 9.8), relies on client-side authentication logic an unauthenticated user can simply reproduce to mint valid requests (CVE-2026-71187, CVSS 9.8), and sends MQTT credentials and control traffic in cleartext (CVE-2026-69658, CVSS 9.8). The remainder cover cleartext web transport, unprotected session tokens, cross-site request forgery, clickjacking, missing server-side authorisation and no login rate limiting. The practical impact is complete unauthorised administrative access, configuration modification, session hijack and loss of device availability. The part that changes your response: CISA records that Ebyte acknowledged the reports and said a patch was under development, then stopped responding. There is no confirmed fix, so this is a mitigate-by-isolation and plan-for-replacement item, not something to add to the patch queue. No public exploitation has been reported to CISA. On 27 August CISA followed up with ICSA-26-239-05 covering a second Ebyte gateway, the NA111-M on firmware 9013-2-17, carrying the same core defect — a web management interface that does not consistently enforce authentication before granting administrative access. Treat the pattern, not the model number, as the finding: if one of these converters is on your network, assume the rest of the range behaves the same way. The same 27 August batch carried ICSA-26-239-03 for Rockwell Automation OTTO Fleet Manager (through V2.36.2), where a weak bcrypt work factor makes stored password hashes cheaper to brute-force offline — lower urgency, but worth pairing with a credential rotation on any OTTO deployment. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-237-06 and ICSA-26-239-05 (Ebyte) and ICSA-26-239-03 (Rockwell Automation OTTO Fleet Manager); NE2-D11 issues reported by researcher Jithin Nambiar — via CISA - NE2-D11 advisory published 25 Aug 2026; NA111-M and OTTO Fleet Manager advisories published 27 Aug 2026; re-verified 28 Aug 2026 — no Ebyte patch announced

item.title: [Critical] The NetScaler KEV deadline is tomorrow — and web shells are already landing on the appliance
item.category: Remote access — Citrix NetScaler ADC / Gateway
item.description: Updated 28 August: the federal clock on CVE-2026-8452 runs out tomorrow. CISA added the flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, one of six additions that day, set a 29 August remediation deadline for federal agencies — the shortest clock it has given a NetScaler flaw this year — and followed up on 27 August urging agencies to patch immediately. Responders report attackers dropping web shells named x.php and z.php and running basic discovery commands, from at least three IP addresses in three countries. Citrix disclosed the bug on 30 June as a memory overflow causing denial of service and patched it the same day; watchTowr then showed on 14 August that it chains into unauthenticated remote code execution, and exploitation began shortly after the write-up. Citrix’s own advisory still does not acknowledge in-the-wild use. Only appliances configured as a Gateway (SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN, RDP Proxy) or AAA virtual server are affected — which is precisely the configuration plants use for engineer and integrator remote access. The separate CVE-2026-19490 authentication bypass disclosed 19 August remains without confirmed exploitation. - CISA KEV catalogue addition and Citrix bulletin CTX696604 — reported by Help Net Security, SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer and Infosecurity Magazine - Citrix advisory and patch 30 Jun 2026; RCE write-up and PoC 14 Aug 2026; KEV addition 26 Aug 2026; exploitation reporting 27 Aug 2026; federal deadline 29 Aug 2026 — re-verified 28 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] A truck brake ECU takes remote code — and the fix shipped two years ago as a safety recall nobody read as security
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-237-05 on 25 August covering the Bendix EC80 electronic control unit, the module that runs anti-lock braking, traction control and stability functions on heavy commercial vehicles including tractor units, buses and school buses. The advisory describes a stack-based buffer overflow that crashes the ECU, and a crafted payload that allows remote code execution or injection of arbitrary CAN bus traffic. Successful exploitation is described as causing loss of ABS, steering assist, speedometer, shifting capability, or disabling automatic traction control. The uncomfortable finding sits in the history rather than the CVE: three vehicle manufacturers recalled roughly 450,000 units in late 2024 for a memory-corruption defect described publicly as a reliability issue, and that recall firmware silently closed the remotely reachable code execution path. Fleets that deferred the recall as a nuisance have been running an exploitable safety controller for two years. No public exploitation has been reported to CISA. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-237-05 — corroborated by SecurityWeek and NMFTA - Published 25 Aug 2026; underlying recall issued 2024

item.title: [High] Hard-coded credentials in a Class B AIS transponder let anyone aboard change the vessel’s identity — and it is end of life
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-237-07 on 25 August for the FURUNO FA-50 Class B AIS transponder, drawing on JPCERT/CC coordination. All versions carry hard-coded credentials (CVE-2026-59769, CVSS 9.1) that let anyone who knows them and can reach the vessel’s internal network open the settings screen and change the identification number the transponder broadcasts. A second flaw allows some management-screen configuration to be altered with no authentication at all (CVE-2026-67578, CVSS 7.5). Production ended in October 2020 and FURUNO states no software updates will be provided, so there is no patch. The operational consequence is identity rather than propulsion: a unit broadcasting the wrong MMSI misrepresents the vessel to every receiver in range and to shore-side traffic services, which is a collision-avoidance and compliance problem before it is a security one. FURUNO advises keeping the device off the internet and physically securing the vessel. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-237-07 — corroborated by JPCERT/CC JVNVU#95422936 - Published 25 Aug 2026; no fix available

item.title: [High] Three more flaws go into KEV today — and the Linux kernel one lives on the appliances watching your process
item.category: Exploited in the wild — OT-adjacent infrastructure
item.description: CISA added three vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 27 August: a Linux kernel privilege-escalation flaw reachable through the IPv6 networking subsystem (CVE-2026-53362), an ownCloud improper-authentication flaw allowing unauthenticated read, write or deletion of any file (CVE-2023-49105), and a path-traversal issue in JFrog Artifactory that lets an authenticated user write outside the intended Docker cache path (CVE-2026-66384). None is an ICS product, and that is exactly why it is worth ten minutes of an OT engineer’s attention. The kernel flaw affects distributions across the Red Hat and SUSE families, which is the software underneath a large share of the passive monitoring sensors, historians, jump hosts, industrial edge gateways and virtualisation hosts sitting inside plant networks — appliances whose patching is contractually the vendor’s job and practically nobody’s. Federal civilian agencies face a three-week remediation deadline; everyone else should treat the appliance question as the actionable part. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition — CISA alert of 27 Aug 2026 - Added 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] A national emergency declaration puts foreign-made grid equipment — and the software inside it — under federal control
item.description: An executive order signed on 26 August declares a national emergency under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and the National Emergencies Act over foreign-produced bulk-power system electric equipment. It generally prohibits, or attaches conditions to, the purchase and installation of covered equipment where the Secretary of Energy determines an undue risk of sabotage, unauthorised access or catastrophic effect on critical infrastructure — and the order explicitly reaches the associated critical software and digital capabilities, not only the iron. Facilities used for local distribution are outside scope. The Secretary is directed to publish implementing rules, to identify equipment that carries the risks described, and — the provision asset owners should read twice — may impose conditions on the continued use and operation of equipment already installed, weighing reliability, safety, availability of replacements and continuity of service. Nothing is enforceable against a named vendor today; the rules do not yet exist. But this converts a procurement question into an inventory question, and the inventory is the part most utilities cannot currently produce. - The White House — executive order and accompanying fact sheet - Signed and published 26 Aug 2026; DOE implementing rules pending; verified against the primary text 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA puts a number on the boring problem: a quarter of critical-infrastructure entities it scanned were exposing vulnerable network services
item.category: Policy — Secure by Design / vulnerability management
item.description: CISA published its Vulnerability Review for fiscal years 2024 and 2025 on 26 August, and buried in a document mostly aimed at software producers is the figure operators should take to their next risk meeting: 26% of critical-infrastructure entities CISA scanned across the two years were exposing vulnerable network services to the internet. Roughly 18% were running FTP — unencrypted, credentials in clear text — with RDP, SMB and Telnet close behind. The review also separates the vulnerabilities that get exploited from the ones that merely get counted: memory-safety and improper-input-validation weaknesses accounted for 19.7% of KEV entries in FY2024 and 16.7% in FY2025, while injection flaws dominate raw CVE volume but rarely succeed against a mature environment. CISA designated 520 CVEs for action across critical-infrastructure entities in the period, and reports that while KEV patching is getting faster, most organisations still miss the recommended remediation windows. The other half of the document is procurement: the Secure by Demand questions are a ready-made vendor questionnaire, and the 2026 SBOM Minimum Elements add data fields to the 2021 NTIA baseline. - CISA Vulnerability Review: Fiscal Years 2024 and 2025 — reported by Industrial Cyber - Published 26 Aug 2026; reported 27 Aug 2026; verified 28 Aug 2026
